## StandardDrawing.kt { #standarddrawing-kt }

The small vocabulary of `FLine` construction and styling that sketches and examples reach for
first.

`fline` is the builder; the `rangeTo` operator makes a one-segment line out of two vectors
(`a..b`, composable with `+=`), and the styling overloads of `moveTo` / `lineTo` / `cubicTo`
position a node and style it in the same call. Appearance is carried by delegated properties on
`FLine` and `FLine.Node` — `color`, `thickness`, `thicken`, `filled`, `stroked`, `pointed`,
`pointSize` — which the renderers read back; `onClick` and `hoverColor` only do anything in the
interactive outputs.

The rest are shape helpers: `rect` and `Rect.toFLine`, `arrow` (a real filled arrowhead rather
than a point sprite), `seg`, and `fitInto`, which scales and centres a list of lines into a
`Rect` using their 2D bounds only.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/StandardDrawing.kt`

**Used in:** [FLine examples (Field graphics)](../fline_examples.md), [Typography as geometry — a string becomes contours](../typography_examples.md), [Points into structure — Voronoi, Apollonius, contours and clusters](../spatial_geometry_examples.md)

### FLineHitKind { #standarddrawing-kt-flinehitkind }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">FLineHitKind</span></code>

What kind of thing on a figure a click landed on — the same three-way distinction the editable FLine widget already draws its hit targets with (`data-fline-hit-kind` in `sliders.js`), now reported to `FLine.onClick` as well.

Constants: `and`, `with`.

### FLineFaceCoordinates { #standarddrawing-kt-flinefacecoordinates }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">FLineFaceCoordinates</span></code>

Which convention `FLineIntersection.u` and `v` follow for a `FLineHitKind.FACE` hit — because there is no one right answer for a face nobody chose, and a plausible wrong number is worse than a labelled one.

Constants: `or`, `so`, `and`, `monotone`.

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">lineIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Index of the clicked line within the lines passed to that one `lines(...)` call, or `-1` when unknown. The point of it: one shared `onClick` closure can serve a whole figure, instead of one closure per part. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">label</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The clicked line's `FLine.label`, if it had one. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">nodeIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Index into the line's `nodes` of the node that *is* this element: the node itself for a `FLineHitKind.POINT`, the node that draws the segment for an `FLineHitKind.EDGE`, the `Close` for a `FLineHitKind.FACE`. `-1` when unknown. Unlike `closestVertexIndex` this is the element, not the nearest dot. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">subPathIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Which subpath (`moveTo`-delimited piece) of the line the element belongs to, or `-1`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">elementIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Ordinal of the element among its own kind within the line — edge 0, 1, 2…; face 0, 1… Or `-1`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">u</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Where on the element the click landed, `0..1`, or `NaN` when it does not apply. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">v</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | The second face coordinate for an `FLineHitKind.FACE`, `NaN` otherwise. See `faceCoordinates`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">faceCoordinates</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">FLineFaceCoordinates</span></code> | Which convention `u` and `v` follow for a face hit — bilinear on a four-corner face, its bounding box otherwise, or a refusal. Always `FLineFaceCoordinates.NONE` for a non-face hit. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">onElement</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec3</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The point *on* the element nearest the click, in the line's own coordinate space, or `null`. |

## colors.kt { #colors-kt }

Colour constructors for the stdlib. Everything here returns a `Vec4` of sRGB-encoded components
clamped to `[0,1]` with alpha last, so the results drop straight into FLine colours and uniforms.

`rgb` / `rgba` accept either 0..1 or 0..255 components — the scale is inferred per call from
whether any component exceeds 1 — and `rgb255` forces the 0..255 reading. `hsl` is HSL with the
usual cube geometry, but the result is encoded through the sRGB transfer function on the way out,
so it is *not* interchangeable with CSS `hsl()` — see `hsl` for what that costs. `okhsl` and
`okhsv` are the Oklab-based equivalents; of the two only `okhsl` holds perceived lightness steady
across hue, because `okhsv` scales `v` against the per-hue gamut cusp exactly as HSV always has.
Hue may be given as a fraction of a turn or in degrees (magnitude above 1 is divided
by 360) and is wrapped either way.

For sets: `hueSetHsl`, `hueSetOkhsl` and `hueSetOkhsv` (aliased `hslSet`, `okhslSet`, `okhsvSet`)
space equally-separated hues around the wheel at a fixed saturation and lightness.
`paletteForBackground` starts from the same okhsl ring but then walks each entry's lightness up
or down until it clears a minimum WCAG contrast ratio against the supplied background, returning
the highest-contrast candidate it found when it cannot reach the target.

## contours.kt { #contours-kt }

Marching-squares iso-contours for 2D scalar fields, plus the scalar field most callers want to
contour.

A field is just a [`ScalarField2D`](graphics.md#contours-kt-scalarfield2d), `(Double, Double) -> Double`. `pointEdgeScalarField2D` builds
one from points and edges — or from a 2D `FLine` — as the union of weighted discs and capsules,
signed so that `iso = 0.0` is the tube boundary; it re-reads the supplied point list on every
sample, so mutating those `Vec2`s moves the field live. `generateIsoContours` samples a field on
an `nx` by `ny` grid and returns stitched polylines, `generateIsoContoursWithStep` takes a target
cell size instead, and the `FLine` overloads choose the sampling window from the line's 2D bounds
grown by the tube radius.

`smoothIsoContours` and `generateSmoothIsoContours` fit cubic splines through the polylines,
treating a contour that ends on the sampling bounds as open and the rest as closed loops.

### Varying the radius along the line — weights

A tube of one radius is `pointRadius`/`edgeRadius`. To make it *taper*, weight the primitives:
every function that builds a point/edge field takes a **weight callback** rather than a list of
weights. On an explicit graph that is [`PointEdgeWeight`](graphics.md#contours-kt-pointedgeweight), `(index, point) -> Double`, indexed the
same way as the `points` you passed in. On an `FLine` it is [`FLinePointWeight`](graphics.md#contours-kt-flinepointweight),
`(nodeIndex, point) -> Double`, where `nodeIndex` is the *fractional* drawing-instruction index of
the flattened point — integral at a `moveTo`/`lineTo`, and interpolated across a `cubicTo`, which
is the same quantity `FLine.uniform_linearize` hands its callback and `linesOut` uses to look up
per-node colour. `FLine.isoWeights` is the stock implementation: it reads a per-node property and
interpolates between the nodes that set it.

These used to be two `List<Double>?` parameters, `pointWeights` and `edgeWeights`, sized against
the points and edges. On the `FLine` overloads that was unusable and not just awkward: the counts
belonged to the *internal* flattening, and the edge count is not even a function of the node
counts, because `pointEdgeGraph2D` drops an edge between near-coincident samples. A caller could
only guess and read the `IllegalArgumentException`. A callback removes the question — and it
survives a change to `samplesPerCubic`, which a list of weights could not.

An edge's weight is always the **minimum** of its two endpoints'. A capsule has one radius for its
whole length and so cannot taper: the taper comes from the union of densely sampled discs, and the
edges only bridge the gaps between them. Taking the *maximum* would let a capsule bulge past the
disc envelope exactly where the weight changes fastest; the minimum fills the gap without ever
fattening it.

### The sign convention, and why it is asymmetric

A grid corner is *inside* iff its sample is **strictly below** `iso`; a sample exactly *at* `iso`
counts as outside. That asymmetry is deliberate and it matters: with a symmetric test (`below`
on one end and `above` on the other, so "equal" is neither) a sample landing exactly on the iso
level suppresses the crossing on *every* edge out of that corner, and the contour silently
vanishes or shatters. It is not an exotic case — `f(x, y) = x` at `iso = 0.0` on any grid with an
odd number of columns of samples used to return **no contour at all**, and the unit circle
sampled over `[-2, 2]` at `nx = ny = 16` came back as four disconnected arcs, severed at the four
points where the circle passes through a grid corner. See `ISO_CROSSING_EPSILON` for the second
half of the same fix, and `marchingCubes` in `mesh_sdf.kt` for the 3D marcher, which uses the
same convention for the same reason.

### What the change to the marcher does and does not touch

Three things changed here at once, and they have very different reach. Measured old-against-new
over 392 (field, resolution, iso) combinations across eight fields:

| change | when it can alter the output | how much |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the two-valued `inside` test | **only** when some grid sample is exactly equal to `iso` | unbounded — a whole contour appears where there was none, or four arcs become one loop. 96 of the 392 cases; **0** cases with no exactly-on-`iso` sample changed |
| `ISO_CROSSING_EPSILON` | when a crossing lands within a thousandth of a cell of a grid corner | at most `1e-3` of a cell edge, an *analytic* bound; the sweep attained `9.93e-4` of a cell |
| the saddle decider | any cell with four crossings whose bilinear saddle disagrees with the old fixed pairing — including on perfectly smooth fields | two segments are re-routed within that one cell, so up to about a cell |

So only the third one reaches ordinary, non-degenerate input, and it reaches it rarely: 4 of the
392 cases, all of them the one saddle cell of `f = x*y`.

### The saddle cell

The four-crossing cell is resolved by the *asymptotic decider*: the sign of the cell's bilinear
saddle value decides which diagonal pair of corners the centre of the cell belongs to. It is a pure
function of the cell's own four corner values, so two cells sharing an edge cannot disagree about
the crossing on it — which is the property the stitcher needs and the old fixed pairing did not
have. It is *not* a claim that the ambiguity has gone away: when the saddle value is exactly `iso`
the two pairings are equally correct and the decider genuinely has nothing to go on. That case is
settled deterministically rather than by round-off — see `SADDLE_TIE_RELATIVE_EPSILON`, which is
where the interesting failure was.

The one remaining roughness: the segment stitcher is O(m^2) in the number of segments, so very
high grid resolutions get expensive.

## fline_graph_connectivity.kt { #fline-graph-connectivity-kt }

Bridge from drawn geometry to the graph algorithms: turns one or more `FLine`s into a welded
point graph.

`flineGraph`, or the `toFLineGraph` extensions on `FLine` and `Iterable<FLine>`, adaptively
subdivides cubics down to `cubicFlatness`, samples every node, then welds samples closer than
`epsilon` using a uniform grid plus union-find (`epsilon = 0` welds only bit-identical
positions). A welded vertex is the mean of the samples that reached it, and
`FLineGraph.vertexSources` records which line index and node instruction each of those samples
came from. Edges join consecutive samples, `close()` joins back to the subpath start,
self-edges are dropped and duplicates collapse to the shortest.

The result carries a `PointGraph` of `GraphEdge`s — the same types as `graph_connectivity.kt` —
so the search, spanning-tree and analysis functions there apply directly to a drawing.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/fline_graph_connectivity.kt`

## graph_connectivity.kt { #graph-connectivity-kt }

Self-contained graph / computational-geometry library over 2D and 3D point sets
(`Vec2`/`Vec3`). Every algorithm has a `vec2*` and (where meaningful) a `vec3*` entry point
returning a [`PointGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt-pointgraph); see each function's own KDoc for its definition and complexity.

Proximity / neighbourhood families: KNN (`vec2KnnGraph`), Orthant (`vec2OrthantGraph`),
Relative Neighborhood (`vec2RelativeNeighborhoodGraph`), Gabriel (`vec2GabrielGraph`),
Beta-Skeleton (`vec2BetaSkeleton`), Nearest-Neighbor (`vec2NearestNeighborGraph`),
Minimum Spanning Tree (`vec2MinimumSpanningTree`), Maximum-Diameter/radius
(`vec2MaximumDiameterGraph`), Maximum-Cut (`vec2MaximumCutGraph`) and Complete
(`vec2CompleteGraph`) graphs.

JTS-backed (2D only): full Delaunay triangulation (`vec2DelaunayGraph`, `vec2DelaunayTriangles`),
Urquhart (`vec2UrquhartGraph`, a real Urquhart graph built by removing the longest edge of each
Delaunay triangle — the 3D `vec3UrquhartGraph` is an MST approximation because Field only wires
2D Delaunay), Voronoi diagram/dual (`vec2VoronoiDiagram`, `vec2VoronoiDualGraph`) and convex
hull (`vec2ConvexHull`, `vec2ConvexHullGraph`, `vec2HullProjectionGraph`).

Traversal / analysis: BFS/DFS/A* path search, [`GraphEdgeVisitState`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt-graphedgevisitstate) greedy walks and
graph-diameter path decomposition (see the search/path functions below), plus FLine rendering
integration in `fline_graph_connectivity.kt`.

Custom distance metrics: pass `GraphConnectivityOptions.customDistanceMetric`. It is honoured by
the distance-driven algorithms (KNN, MST, RNG, Gabriel, Beta-Skeleton, Delaunay/Urquhart edge
weights, etc.). This includes `vec2OrthantGraph`/`vec3OrthantGraph`, whose nearest-neighbour
ranking within each orthant honours `customDistanceMetric` when supplied (Euclidean otherwise).

Smoke tests: `afield.examples.stdlib.GraphConnectivitySmokeTest` (its `runTests()` drives 35
checks, covering path search, edge-visit-state and FLine rendering as well as the core graphs).
Live rendered examples: `public/docs/graph_connectivity_examples.md`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/graph_connectivity.kt`

**Used in:** [Neighbors & graph connectivity to FLine examples](../graph_connectivity_examples.md), [Points into structure — Voronoi, Apollonius, contours and clusters](../spatial_geometry_examples.md)

## keyframer.kt { #keyframer-kt }

Snapshot, interpolate and persist the live state of a running sketch. A [`KeyframeScope`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keyframescope) is a set
of named targets — uniform `Structure` bindings, the uniform structures of a `ModulePointer` /
`ComputeModulePointer` / `MeshModulePointer`, a stackAuto shader-source slot via
`KeyframeScope.stackAuto`, or a `Camera` pose via `KeyframeScope.camera`. `capture()` reads them
all into a `KeyframeScope.Key`; invoking that `Key` writes them all back.

`KeyframeScope.interpolate` blends two keys per value type: numbers and vectors lerp, quaternions
slerp, dual quaternions and `CameraPose` sclerp, and strings / [`StackSLString`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-stackslstring) /
`SourceBackedBlock` step to the right-hand value at `t >= 1`. `remap` can re-time an individual
key's `t`.

Persistence goes through the [`KValue`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-kvalue) serial union, so only the types `KValue.fromAny` recognises
survive a save — numbers, vec2/3/4, quaternion, dual quaternion, camera pose, string, StackSL
source and source-backed block; anything else is silently dropped. Every `saveKey` also writes a
numbered copy into a `<file>.versions` directory with a manifest, which
`KeyframeScope.keyVersions` lists and `KeyframeScope.loadLatestKey` follows. `KeyframeScope.missingKey` supplies defaults for
keys absent from an older file, optionally per schema version.

Keys render themselves as HTML for box output ([`KeyDiff`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keydiff), `diffHtml`), and
`copyUpdateCodeToClipboard` emits pasteable Kotlin — that one goes through the AWT clipboard.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/keyframer.kt`

**Used in:** [Keyframes: capturing, persisting and replaying live state](../keyframer_examples.md), [Values over time: interpolants & keyframes](../interpolants_examples.md)

### NumKind { #keyframer-kt-numkind }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">NumKind</span></code>

Which Kotlin numeric type a saved number came from, so that `KValue.toAny` can hand back a `Byte`/`Short`/`Int`/`Long`/`Float`/`Double` rather than always a `Double` — a uniform bound to an `Int` has to come back as an `Int`.

Constants: `BYTE`, `SHORT`, `INT`, `LONG`, `FLOAT`, `DOUBLE`.

### KValue { #keyframer-kt-kvalue }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">sealed</span> <span class="k">interface</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code>

The closed set of value types a `KeyframeScope.Key` can *persist*: numbers, vec2/3/4, quaternion, dual quaternion, camera pose, string, StackSL source and source-backed block. A key in memory holds plain Kotlin values; this is the serial union they are converted to on the way to disk and back.

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Vec3</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">z</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | A `Vector3f`, component by component. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Vec4</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">z</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">w</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | A `Vector4f`, component by component — the usual RGBA or homogeneous-point uniform. |

Unlike [`Quat`](math.md#linalg-kt-quat) this *is* normalised on the way back in, so a slightly drifted saved value is repaired on load. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">CameraPoseValue</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">realX</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">realY</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">realZ</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">realW</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dualX</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dualY</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dualZ</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dualW</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">focusDistance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | A `CameraPose`: the camera's rigid transform as a dual quaternion, plus the focus distance that says how far in front of it the thing it is looking at sits. Also normalised on load. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">StackSL</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | StackSL source text, tagged as code rather than as a string so that it reloads as a [`StackSLString`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-stackslstring) and interpolation steps it discretely instead of trying to blend it. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Str</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | A plain `String`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">SourceBlock</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">boxId</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">source</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | A `SourceBackedBlock` reduced to the box it came from and its Kotlin source — the *live lambda* is not persisted. On load the block re-compiles its source in that box on first invocation, so a key restored into a document where the box is gone throws when the value is finally called. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">toAny</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span></code> | Rebuild the live Kotlin value this entry stands for — the load half of the round trip. A [`DualQuat`](math.md#linalg-kt-dualquat) and a `CameraPoseValue` are re-normalised on the way out, because a rigid transform that has drifted is a broken transform; a plain [`Quat`](math.md#linalg-kt-quat) deliberately is **not** (see its own note — it may be standing in for something that is not a rotation). Numbers regain their [`NumKind`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-numkind) type, and a `SourceBlock` becomes a `SourceBackedBlock` that has not compiled anything yet. |

### KeyDTO { #keyframer-kt-keydto }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">KeyDTO</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">schemaVersion</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Map</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

Nothing validates it on load: a mismatch is not an error, it only selects which `KeyframeScope.missingKey` defaults apply. |

### KeyVersionInfo { #keyframer-kt-keyversioninfo }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">KeyVersionInfo</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">index</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">timestamp</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">note</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">file</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

One row of a key file's version history, as recorded in the `<file>.versions/manifest.json` that every `saveKey` appends to. `KeyframeScope.keyVersions` hands these back, sorted by `index`.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">index</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Monotonic version number, starting at 0 and simply "highest so far plus one" — a save counter, not a schema version and not related to `KeyDTO.schemaVersion`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">timestamp</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | When the version was written, as an ISO-8601 `Instant.now()` string in UTC — or, for a row rebuilt from the file alone, that file's last-modified time. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">note</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Whatever note was passed to `saveKey`, for telling two snapshots apart later. A row rebuilt from the file alone says `"(recovered from disk; the manifest row for this version was lost)"` here instead, since the real note lived only in the manifest that went missing. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">file</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | File name inside the `.versions` directory, `"%06d.json"` of `index`. |

### StackSLString { #keyframer-kt-stackslstring }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">StackSLString</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

### KeyframeScope { #keyframer-kt-keyframescope }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">KeyframeScope</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">schemaVersion</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

A named set of live things worth snapshotting — uniform `Structure` bindings, a module's live uniforms, a `stack.auto` shader slot, a `Camera` — plus the machinery to capture, blend, save and reload them. This is the object you keep around for the lifetime of a sketch.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">targets</span></code> | The statically-bound targets, by key name, as registered by `target(name, structure)` — exposed so you can see and clear what a scope is watching. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">remap</span></code> | Per-key re-timing for `interpolate`: `remap["gain"] = { t -> t * t * (3 - 2 * t) }` eases that one value on a smoothstep while everything else stays linear. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">inner</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Key</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MutableMap</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ToHTML</span></code> | One snapshot: names to values, and the ability to put them all back. Get one from `capture`, `interpolate`, `loadKey`, or by constructing it from a map you wrote by hand (as the docs examples do). |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">target</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">structure</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Structure</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Register a key `name` against a uniform `structure` held for good — the simplest target, for a `Structure` you built once and will keep. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">target</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">structure</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Structure</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Register a key `name` against a structure that is looked up **again on every read and write** — the right choice for anything a shader reload can replace underneath you. |

Evaluated at most once per load, and **only when the file actually lacks the name** — a default whose name the file already carries is never called at all. |

Reading only: nothing is applied to the sketch until you invoke the returned key. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">loadLatestKey</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">path</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Path</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Key</span></code> | The highest-numbered entry of `path`'s version history, falling back to `path` itself when there is no history at all. |

### KeyDiffKind { #keyframer-kt-keydiffkind }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">KeyDiffKind</span></code>

How one name differs between two keys, always read left-to-right: `ADDED` means the right key has it and the left does not, `REMOVED` the other way round, `CHANGED` that both have it with unequal values. There is no "same" kind — unchanged names are left out of a diff entirely.

Constants: `ADDED`, `REMOVED`, `CHANGED`.

### KeyDiffEntry { #keyframer-kt-keydiffentry }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">KeyDiffEntry</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">kind</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KeyDiffKind</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">left</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">right</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

One line of a [`KeyDiff`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keydiff): what the name was on each side, and which way it moved.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | The key name, as it appears in both snapshots (`@`-qualified if that is how it was registered). |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">kind</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KeyDiffKind</span></code> | Whether this name was added, removed, or changed between left and right. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">left</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The left-hand value; null for an `ADDED` entry, which had none. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">right</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The right-hand value; null for a `REMOVED` entry. |

### KeyDiff { #keyframer-kt-keydiff }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">KeyDiff</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">leftName</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">rightName</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">entries</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">KeyDiffEntry</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ToHTML</span></code>

The difference between two `KeyframeScope.Key`s: only the names that actually moved, sorted by name, ready to render. Produced by `Key.diff`.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">leftName</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | Heading for the left-hand column — cosmetic, defaulting to `"left"` at the call site. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">rightName</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | Heading for the right-hand column. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">entries</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">KeyDiffEntry</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | The changes, name-sorted; empty means the two keys agree. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">toString</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | The diff as text, one line per change prefixed `+` (added), `-` (removed) or `~` (changed), and the single line "No key differences." when there are none. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">toHTML</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | The diff as a small dark-mode HTML table — one row per change, marker coloured green for added, red for removed and amber for changed, with a header counting the changes. What a box shows when a `KeyDiff` is the value on screen. |

## mesh.kt { #mesh-kt }

[`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) — the CPU triangle mesh Field's 3D geometry family is built on, plus the builder that
makes one and the whole-mesh transforms that move one around.

A [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) is deliberately *not* a renderer buffer (that is `afield.four`'s
`afield.four.modules.Mesh`) and deliberately *not* a graph of vertex objects. It is flat
`FloatArray` attribute storage plus an `IntArray` of triangle indices: the layout every algorithm
in this family wants, the layout a GPU upload wants, and cheap to copy. Positions are required;
normals, uvs and per-vertex colours are optional and either absent or complete.

The reason the vertices are floats-in-an-array rather than `List<Vec3>` is that `Vec3` is a
*mutable* `Vector3f`. A mesh holding shared mutable vectors is a mesh where `mesh.position(0).y +=
1` silently edits the mesh — or worse, edits three triangles because the vector was shared. So
every accessor here (`position`, `normal`, `uv`, `color`) returns a **fresh** vector you own, and
the `…Into` variants let a hot loop reuse one.

### The family

| file | what it adds |
|---|---|
| `mesh.kt` | this: the type, [`TriMeshBuilder`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimeshbuilder) / `triMesh`, transforms, concatenation |
| `mesh_topology.kt` | [`MeshTopology`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt-meshtopology) — adjacency, boundary loops, components, manifoldness, Euler characteristic / genus, `TriMesh.weld`, `TriMesh.fixWinding` |
| `mesh_generate.kt` | `boxMesh`, `uvSphereMesh`, `icosphereMesh`, `torusMesh`, `cylinderMesh`, `extrudeMesh`, `revolveMesh`, `tubeMesh`, `heightfieldMesh` |
| `mesh_sdf.kt` | [`ScalarField3D`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt-scalarfield3d), the SDF primitives / combinators, and `marchingCubes` |
| `mesh_process.kt` | `TriMesh.loopSubdivide`, `TriMesh.laplacianSmooth`, `TriMesh.taubinSmooth`, `TriMesh.withVertexNormals`, `TriMesh.decimate` |
| `mesh_measure.kt` | `TriMesh.surfaceArea`, `TriMesh.signedVolume`, curvature, [`MeshBvh`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt-meshbvh) (rays, closest point, inside test) |
| `mesh_io.kt` | OBJ and STL, read and write |
| `mesh_field.kt` | the bridges: `TriMesh.toFLines`, `VoronoiCell3.toTriMesh`, `Box.showMesh` |

### Conventions

- **Winding is counter-clockwise seen from outside**, so `faceNormal` points out of a closed
  solid and `signedVolume` of one is positive. Everything in the family agrees on this, and
  `TriMesh.fixWinding` repairs a mesh that does not.
- Nothing here mutates: every operation returns a new [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh). The arrays are `val`s and are
  not copied on construction, so do not hand a builder's scratch array to the constructor and
  then keep writing to it — use `TriMeshBuilder.build`.
- No dependencies beyond the Kotlin stdlib and Field's own generated linalg. No GPU, no AWT, no
  model-format libraries.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val ball = icosphereMesh(subdivisions = 3, radius = 1.0)
val shell = ball.scaled(1.0, 0.6, 1.0).withVertexNormals()
println("${shell.triangleCount} tris, volume ${shell.signedVolume()}")
display(shell.toFLines())            // draw its wireframe
```

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/mesh.kt`

**Used in:** [Meshes and 3D geometry](../mesh_examples.md)

### TriMeshBuilder { #mesh-kt-trimeshbuilder }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">TriMeshBuilder</span></code>

The accumulator every generator in this family is written against: append vertices, append triangles that reference them, `build`.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">vertexCount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How many vertices have been appended so far — also the index the next `vertex` will get. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">triangleCount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How many triangles have been appended so far. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">vertex</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">p</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec3</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">normal</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec3</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">uv</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec2</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">color</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec3</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Append a vertex and return its index. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">vertex</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">z</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">normal</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec3</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">uv</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec2</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">color</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec3</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | `vertex` from loose floats — what the generators use, so they never allocate a `Vec3` per vertex. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">triangle</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">c</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Append one triangle. Counter-clockwise seen from outside. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">quad</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">c</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">d</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Append a quad as two triangles: `(a,b,c)` and `(a,c,d)`. Corners in order around the quad. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">polygon</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">corners</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Append a convex polygon as a fan from its first corner. Non-convex polygons will self-overlap — `extrudeMesh` triangulates properly via ear clipping for those. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">add</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">mesh</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">TriMesh</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Append a whole mesh, offsetting its indices. Returns the index its vertex 0 landed on. |

The builder stays usable; the mesh gets its own arrays. |

## mesh_field.kt { #mesh-field-kt }

What makes the mesh family *Field's* rather than a generic geometry library: the bridges out of
[`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) and into the things Field already draws, renders and displays.

Four bridges:

 1. **Mesh → `FLine`.** `TriMesh.toFLines` gives you the wireframe, the silhouette-free edge set,
    the open boundary loops or the normals as drawable lines, so a marched iso-surface goes
    straight into the same drawing / animation / export machinery as anything hand-drawn — and is
    visible in a Field document *today*, with no renderer set up.
 2. **Mesh → pixels.** `TriMesh.renderPng` rasterises the mesh — perspective, z-buffer,
    perspective-correct attributes, two-light lambert, depth-tested wireframe — by packing it for
    `VisionGeometryPreview`'s renderer, which already had all of that. `Box.showMesh` pushes the
    result to a box output and `TriMesh.toHTML` uses it for the inline value thumbnail, so
    evaluating a mesh in a box shows the shape.
 3. **3D Voronoi → mesh.** `VoronoiCell3.toTriMesh` and `VoronoiLattice.toTriMesh` triangulate the
    polygonal cells `voronoi.kt` already computes by half-space clipping. Field could compute a 3D
    Voronoi diagram and not turn it into geometry; now it can.
 4. **Field lines → mesh.** `tubeMesh` on an `FLine`, so a drawn stroke becomes a solid.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val cells = voronoi3d(List(24) { vec(rand(-1, 1), rand(-1, 1), rand(-1, 1)) })
val solid = cells.toTriMesh(shrink = 0.9)   // every cell, shrunk toward its own site
showMesh(solid, caption = "${solid.triangleCount} triangles from 24 sites")
```

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/mesh_field.kt`

**Used in:** [Geometry from disk](../geometry_from_disk.md), [Field's 3D output](../three_output.md), [Meshes and 3D geometry](../mesh_examples.md)

| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">TriMesh</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">toFLines</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">mode</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MeshLines</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">MeshLines</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">EDGES</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">creaseAngleDegrees</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">25.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">normalLength</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.03</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | This mesh as drawable `FLine`s — the fastest way to see a mesh in a Field document without involving a renderer. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">tubeMesh</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">line</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">FLine</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.05</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">sides</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">12</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">samples</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">64</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">closed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">caps</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">true</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">TriMesh</span></code> | A tube swept along an `FLine`, sampled at `samples` points — see `tubeMesh`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">VoronoiCell3</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">toTriMesh</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">shrink</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">fanFromCentroid</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">true</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">healToConvexHull</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">true</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">TriMesh</span></code> | One 3D Voronoi cell's polygonal faces, triangulated into a closed [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh). |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">VoronoiLattice</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">toTriMesh</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">shrink</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.92</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">boundedOnly</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">TriMesh</span></code> | Every cell of a 3D Voronoi lattice as one [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh), one connected component per cell. |

How to draw a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) in a preview: where the camera stands and what the frame looks like.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">yawDegrees</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Orbit around `+y`, in degrees. `0` looks straight down `-z`. |

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">fieldOfViewDegrees</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Vertical field of view in degrees. Smaller is a longer lens and less perspective. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">width</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Output width in pixels. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">height</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Output height in pixels. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">wireframe</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Draw a depth-tested wireframe over the shading. On by default: it turns "a smooth blob" into "a mesh you can count the triangles in". |

## mesh_generate.kt { #mesh-generate-kt }

Where a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) comes from: the primitives (`boxMesh`, `uvSphereMesh`, `icosphereMesh`,
`torusMesh`, `cylinderMesh`, `coneMesh`, `capsuleMesh`, the five platonics) and the *derived*
generators that build one out of something you already have (`extrudeMesh`, `revolveMesh`,
`tubeMesh`, `heightfieldMesh`, `polygonMesh`).

### Two conventions worth knowing before you use any of them

**Everything here is welded and watertight where it can be.** A generator returns the minimal
vertex set, so `MeshTopology.eulerCharacteristic` of a box, a sphere, a cone or a capped cylinder
is exactly `2`, of a torus exactly `0`, and `TriMesh.isWatertight` is true. That is a much stronger
guarantee than "it renders", it is what the volume / curvature / decimation code needs, and it is
checked in the tests.

**Normals are only attached where they are unambiguous.** A sphere, icosphere, torus and capsule
are smooth everywhere, so they carry per-vertex normals. A box, cylinder, cone, extrusion or
platonic solid has *creases*: the two faces meeting at an edge want different normals at the same
vertex, and you cannot have both a shared vertex and two normals. Rather than silently duplicate
the seam (breaking watertightness) or silently average across the crease (rounding it off), these
ship with **no** normals, and you pick:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
boxMesh().flatShaded()          // one normal per triangle: hard edges, 3 verts per tri
boxMesh().shadedNormals(35.0)   // split only where faces disagree by > 35 degrees
boxMesh().withVertexNormals()   // one averaged normal per shared vertex: rounded corners
```

The preview / render bridges in `mesh_field.kt` call `TriMesh.shadedNormals` for you when a mesh
arrives without normals, so a bare `boxMesh()` still looks like a box.

### Orientation

`+y` is up, matching the preview camera. Radial generators sweep `x = r cos u, z = -r sin u`, which
is the handedness that makes counter-clockwise-from-outside windings come out right. `planeMesh`
and `polygonMesh` live in the `xy` plane facing `+z`; `heightfieldMesh` lives in the `xz` plane
facing `+y` — the difference is deliberate, a plane is a wall and a heightfield is a landscape.

## mesh_io.kt { #mesh-io-kt }

Getting a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) in and out of the two formats every 3D tool on the machine can already read:
**OBJ** (text, indexed, carries normals and uvs) and **STL** (ASCII or binary, triangle soup, the
lingua franca of 3D printing).

Both directions, no dependencies, and honest about what each format can carry:

 - `TriMesh.toObj` / `objToTriMesh` keep the index structure, so a watertight mesh round-trips as a
   watertight mesh. Normals and uvs survive; per-vertex colours do not (OBJ has no standard for
   them). Faces with more than three corners are fan-triangulated on read, so a quad-mesh OBJ from
   a modeller loads fine.
 - `TriMesh.toStlAscii` / `TriMesh.toStlBinary` / `stlToTriMesh` are *triangle soup* by design:
   STL has no vertex sharing at all, so a mesh written to STL and read back has `3 *
   triangleCount` vertices and reports every edge as a boundary. `stlToTriMesh(bytes).weld()` gives
   you the mesh back. That is a property of the format, not of this code, and the read path says
   so in its KDoc rather than silently welding for you — welding needs a tolerance, and choosing
   one for you is exactly the kind of guess that loses a hairline feature.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val mesh = icosphereMesh(3)
File("/tmp/ball.obj").writeText(mesh.toObj())
File("/tmp/ball.stl").writeBytes(mesh.toStlBinary())
val back = objToTriMesh(File("/tmp/ball.obj").readText())
```

These two formats, and no others — see `meshFromFile` for where to go for PLY, glTF and GLB, and
`public/docs/geometry_from_disk.md` for the measured account of what each format loses.

## mesh_measure.kt { #mesh-measure-kt }

Asking a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) questions: how big is it, where is its middle, how curved is it — and, through
[`MeshBvh`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt-meshbvh), what does this ray hit, what is the nearest point on the surface, and is this point
inside.

The measurements (`TriMesh.surfaceArea`, `TriMesh.signedVolume`, `TriMesh.centroid`) are exact for
the polyhedron, computed in double precision, and cheap. `TriMesh.signedVolume` is the one to keep
in mind: it is the divergence-theorem tetrahedron sum, so it is exact for any closed mesh, it is
**positive for outward winding and negative for inward**, and comparing it against an analytic
answer (`4/3 π` for a marched unit sphere) is the single most informative test a geometry pipeline
can have.

The curvatures are the standard discrete operators — angle deficit for Gaussian, the
cotangent-Laplacian's magnitude for mean, both divided by the mixed Voronoi area. They satisfy
Gauss-Bonnet (`Σ K_v A_v = 2π χ`) to float precision on a closed mesh, which is how they are tested.

[`MeshBvh`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt-meshbvh) exists because the useful queries are all `O(n)` without it and `O(log n)` with it. It is
a plain median-split bounding-volume hierarchy over triangles, built once, then:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val bvh = mesh.bvh()
bvh.raycast(vec(0, 0, -5), vec(0, 0, 1))?.let { println("hit at ${it.point}") }
bvh.closestPoint(vec(2, 0, 0))                 // nearest surface point + distance
bvh.contains(vec(0, 0, 0))                     // inside test, by parity of crossings
bvh.signedDistance(vec(0.5f, 0, 0))            // negative inside
```

## mesh_process.kt { #mesh-process-kt }

Changing a mesh's *sampling* without changing the shape it stands for: normals, subdivision,
smoothing and decimation.

These are the four operations that make the difference between a mesh you generated and a mesh you
can use. In rough order of how often you will reach for them:

 - `TriMesh.withVertexNormals` / `TriMesh.flatShaded` / `TriMesh.shadedNormals` — shading. The
   third is the interesting one: it splits a vertex only where the faces meeting there genuinely
   disagree, so a cylinder comes out smooth around its side and hard at its rim, from one call.
 - `TriMesh.loopSubdivide` — four triangles for one, converging on the Loop limit surface. Refines
   *and* smooths, and preserves the Euler characteristic exactly.
 - `TriMesh.laplacianSmooth` / `TriMesh.taubinSmooth` — noise removal. Laplacian shrinks the shape
   (that is what a diffusion does); Taubin's λ/μ pair alternates a shrink with an expand and so
   does not, which is why it is the one to default to. Both offer cotangent weights, which are
   scale- and shape-independent where the uniform ones are not.
 - `TriMesh.decimate` — quadric error metric edge collapse down to a triangle budget. The dual of
   subdivision, and the one that has to work hardest: it maintains per-vertex quadrics, a
   cost-ordered queue with lazy invalidation, the link condition (so a collapse cannot make the
   mesh non-manifold) and a normal-flip veto (so it cannot turn the mesh inside out locally).

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val fine = icosphereMesh(4)                       // 5120 triangles
val coarse = fine.decimate(400)                   // 400, and still a sphere
val smooth = coarse.taubinSmooth(iterations = 20) // volume preserved to within ~1%
```

Catmull-Clark is deliberately absent: it is a quad scheme, [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) is triangles-only, and
running it on a triangulated quad mesh gives a different (worse) surface than running it on the
quads. Loop is the triangle scheme, and it is the one here.

## mesh_repair.kt { #mesh-repair-kt }

Why a mesh is not a solid, and what can be done about it — the paved road between "I loaded a file"
and `toSolid()`.

`TriMesh.diagnose` answers *why*, in terms a person can act on: which loops are open and how big,
which edges have the wrong number of faces, which faces are duplicated, whether the winding is
consistent and whether it points out. `TriMesh.repairToSolid` then attempts the fixes in a
defensible order and hands back a [`MeshRepairResult`](graphics.md#mesh-repair-kt-meshrepairresult) that says **what it did and what it could
not do** — a repair that quietly drops half your model is worse than one that refuses, so nothing
here returns a bare mesh.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val mesh = meshFromAnyFile("scan.glb")
println(mesh.diagnose().report())     // why it is not a solid, worst first
val fixed = mesh.repairToSolid()
println(fixed.report())               // what was done, and what was not
if (fixed.isSolid) display(fixed.mesh.toSolid() - drill)
```

### What actually blocks `toSolid`, measured rather than assumed

Every severity below was established by feeding Manifold a mesh damaged in exactly one named way
(see `MeshDamage` in the tests) and asking whether it accepted the result. The answers are not the
ones folklore predicts, and three of them matter:

 - **A mesh with several disjoint components is fine.** Manifold accepts it and reports the sum of
   the volumes. "Split into parts" is not a defect; it is `MeshDefectKind.MULTIPLE_COMPONENTS`, and
   it is informational.
 - **Zero-area triangles are fine.** Manifold accepts them and the volume is unchanged.
 - **An inside-out mesh is fine, and that is the dangerous one.** Manifold accepts a consistently
   but inwardly wound closed surface and reports a **negative volume** — so the boolean you do next
   silently computes the wrong thing rather than throwing. That is
   `MeshDefectKind.INVERTED_ORIENTATION`, and it is the reason this file reports severity
   `MeshDefectSeverity.SUSPICIOUS` at all instead of just a pass/fail.

What Manifold genuinely rejects is a short list: a non-finite position, an edge with other than two
incident faces (which a duplicated face also produces, on all three of its edges), an open boundary,
and inconsistent winding.

### What the existing repairs already do, and where they stop

`TriMesh.repaired` — `weld → removeDegenerateTriangles → removeUnusedVertices → fixWinding` — is
not a straw man. Measured over twelve meshes that Manifold rejected, it already fixes **six**: every
unwelded-seam case (welding is what turns an STL's pile of triangles into a surface) and every
inconsistent-winding case. The six it cannot fix are exactly two families, and they are what this
file adds:

 1. **Open boundaries** — nothing in the old pipeline fills a hole. `fillHoles` is the new code.
 2. **Non-manifold edges** — nothing removes a duplicated face or a dangling fin.
    `removeDuplicateFaces` and `removeNonManifoldFins` are the new code.

So the honest framing is that this file is the *last third* of a mesh repair pipeline, not the whole
of one, and `TriMesh.repairToSolid` calls the existing repairs for the first two thirds.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/mesh_repair.kt`

**Used in:** [Solids that cannot fail: Manifold in Field](../manifold.md), [Geometry from disk](../geometry_from_disk.md)

## mesh_sdf.kt { #mesh-sdf-kt }

Modelling with functions: a [`ScalarField3D`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt-scalarfield3d) is `(Vec3) -> Float`, the signed-distance primitives
and combinators that let you write a shape as an expression, and `marchingCubes`, which turns any
such expression into a watertight [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh).

This is the 3D counterpart of `contours.kt`. There, a [`ScalarField2D`](graphics.md#contours-kt-scalarfield2d) is marched by
`generateIsoContours` into `FLine` polylines; here a [`ScalarField3D`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt-scalarfield3d) is marched into triangles.
The two files are deliberately parallel, and reading the 2D one first is the fastest way to
understand this one.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val body = sdfSmoothUnion(
    sdfSphere(0.8),
    sdfBox(vec(1.4, 0.25, 0.25)),
    k = 0.25,
)
val drilled = sdfSubtract(body, sdfCylinder(0.22, 3.0))
val mesh = marchingCubes(drilled, boundsOf(vec(-1.6, -1.6, -1.6), vec(1.6, 1.6, 1.6)), resolution = 96)
println("${mesh.triangleCount} tris, watertight ${mesh.isWatertight()}")
```

### What `marchingCubes` here actually does

It is a **topologically consistent** marching cubes, not the 1987 lookup table:

 - The field is sampled once per grid corner, so the cost is `(n+1)^3` evaluations however many
   triangles come out.
 - Every crossing sits on a grid *edge*, and edges are keyed globally, so a vertex is created once
   and **shared** by all the cubes that touch it. That is what makes the output watertight
   (`χ = 2` for a marched sphere) rather than a soup of unwelded triangles needing `TriMesh.weld`.
 - Instead of a 256-entry triangle table, each cube's crossings are joined into closed loops on the
   cube's own boundary and each loop is triangulated. On a face where four edges cross — the
   ambiguous case the classic table resolves arbitrarily — the pairing is chosen by the
   **asymptotic decider** (the sign of the bilinear saddle value). Because that decision is a pure
   function of the face's four corner values, the two cubes sharing the face always agree, which is
   exactly the property the classic table lacks and the reason plain marching cubes leaks.
 - Winding comes from the field itself: each triangle is oriented against the gradient of the
   trilinear interpolant, so normals point toward increasing field value — outward, for the
   signed-distance convention where outside is positive.

Known limits, stated rather than hidden: a cube containing two separate sheets of surface can be
oriented from one gradient and get the other sheet backwards, so a field with structure much finer
than the grid wants more resolution; and the loop triangulation reproduces the *sign pattern*
faithfully but is not guaranteed to reproduce the trilinear interpolant's exact topology in the
rarest configurations.

### A note on mutation

`Vec3` is mutable and the march reuses one sample vector for speed. A [`ScalarField3D`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt-scalarfield3d) must
therefore **read** the vector it is handed and not write to it. Every combinator below copies
before transforming, so composing them is safe; a hand-written field that does `p.mul(2f)` will
corrupt the march.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/mesh_sdf.kt`

**Used in:** [Meshes and 3D geometry](../mesh_examples.md), [Field's 3D output](../three_output.md), [Typography as geometry — a string becomes contours](../typography_examples.md)

### ScalarField3D { #mesh-sdf-kt-scalarfield3d }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">typealias</span> <span class="nc">ScalarField3D</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">Vec3</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code>

A scalar field in space: `f(x, y, z)`. For a signed distance function, negative is inside.

## mesh_topology.kt { #mesh-topology-kt }

What a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) *is*, as opposed to where it is: adjacency, boundaries, components,
manifoldness, orientation, and the Euler characteristic those add up to — plus the repairs
(`TriMesh.weld`, `TriMesh.fixWinding`, `TriMesh.removeDegenerateTriangles`) that turn a mesh
which fails those checks into one that passes.

[`MeshTopology`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt-meshtopology) is a **derived, cached** view: building one costs one pass over the triangles, and
everything after that is a lookup. Build it once and ask it many questions; the convenience
properties on [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) (`TriMesh.isWatertight` and friends) build a throwaway one each time,
which is fine interactively and wasteful in a loop.

The interesting invariant, and the one the tests lean on: for a closed orientable surface,
`V - E + F = 2 - 2g`. So a cube, a sphere and an icosphere all report
`MeshTopology.eulerCharacteristic` `2` and `MeshTopology.genus` `0`, a torus reports `0` and `1`,
and a two-holed shape reports `-2` and `2`. That single number catches a startling range of
generator bugs — a duplicated seam, a missing cap, an unwelded march — because all of them change
it.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val t = torusMesh(48, 24)
val topo = t.topology()
println("${topo.eulerCharacteristic} χ, genus ${topo.genus}, watertight ${topo.isWatertight}")
// 0 χ, genus 1, watertight true
```

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/mesh_topology.kt`

**Used in:** [Meshes and 3D geometry](../mesh_examples.md), [Geometry from disk](../geometry_from_disk.md), [Solids that cannot fail: Manifold in Field](../manifold.md)

## modelling.kt { #modelling-kt }

A self-tuning controller for pushing the *distribution* of a scalar signal towards a target
shape. You hand `AdaptiveDistributionController.pushSamples` a batch of samples each frame and it
returns a [`ControlOutput`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-controloutput) whose `appliedParams` are the next parameter values to send to whatever
produced them — a shader, a simulation, a tone curve.

The error signal comes from a [`FeatureExtractor`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-featureextractor); [`UniformQuantileFeatureExtractor`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-uniformquantilefeatureextractor) is the
built-in one and measures how far a set of sample quantiles sit from their targets. Internally
each feature gets a recursive-least-squares row (with forgetting) that learns a local Jacobian,
the step is a Tikhonov-regularised Gauss-Newton solve scaled by a confidence estimate, then
softened near the parameter bounds, rate-limited by `maxStep`, clipped, and finally offset by a
per-parameter sinusoidal dither so the estimator keeps seeing excitation.

`ControllerConfig.observationDelayFrames` is the important knob: it models pipeline latency
explicitly by pairing each observation with the command issued that many pushes earlier, so the
loop does not have to be slowed down to learn correctly. Use [`AdaptiveDistributionControllerBank`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-adaptivedistributioncontrollerbank)
for one controller per scene, and [`AdaptiveDistributionLoop`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-adaptivedistributionloop) to drive `observe`/`apply` from a
`Runloop` hook.

This is plain `DoubleArray` math with no GPU or `Box` dependency; every array in
[`ControllerConfig`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-controllerconfig) must be `parameterNames.size` long. `main` runs a synthetic drifting-Gaussian
plant against the controller and prints a trace.

## quantilewarp.kt { #quantilewarp-kt }

Reshapes a scalar signal's distribution by fitting a monotone 8-knot PCHIP curve from the
measured quantiles of recent samples onto the quantiles of a chosen target distribution —
`TargetDistributions.UnitNormal` by default, or any [`QuantileFunction`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt-quantilefunction).

`AdaptiveQuantileWarp.update` takes a batch of samples, merges it with the last
`historyFrames` batches, and returns a [`QuantileWarpState`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt-quantilewarpstate): the knot pairs, an
`QuantileWarpState.evaluate` for CPU-side use, and the same 16 knots packed into four `vec4`s
ready for push constants via `QuantileWarpState.applyToPushConstants`. Successive states are
smoothed towards each other by `smoothingAlpha` and forced strictly increasing, so the curve
stays invertible even when the input degenerates.

`fieldQuantileWarpIncludeSource` is the matching GLSL — `fieldQuantileWarp8` and
`fieldQuantileWarpMix` evaluate the identical PCHIP curve on the GPU — and is reachable from
shader source as the built-in include named by `FIELD_QUANTILE_WARP_INCLUDE_NAME`.
`Box.fieldProbeQuantileWarp` closes the loop: it installs a runloop hook that drains a
`ShaderFieldProbe`, updates the warp, calls your `apply` callback and renders a knot table into a
box display channel.

Constraints worth knowing: exactly eight strictly increasing probabilities inside `(0, 1)`, and
the `Box.fieldProbeQuantileWarp` entry point needs a live `Box` plus a probe configured for
continuous snapshot reads.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/quantilewarp.kt`

**Used in:** [Which of these signals actually depend on each other?](../statistics_examples.md), [afield.four Graphics](../afield_four_graphics.md)

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">AdaptiveQuantileWarp</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">config</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">QuantileWarpConfig</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">QuantileWarpConfig</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">target</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">QuantileFunction</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">TargetDistributions</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">UnitNormal</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

How `Box.fieldProbeQuantileWarp` drives a warp off a GPU probe: when a batch is big enough to be worth fitting, what to clip, and where to draw the knots.

## shaders.kt { #shaders-kt }

The bridge between a box's text and a live Vulkan pipeline: shader source lives in box
properties, and this file turns it into modules and keeps them hot-reloading.

The properties come first — `vertex`, `fragment`, `compute`, `task`/`mesh`, the ray-tracing
stages, and a `_s` variant of each for Slang — alongside `once.vertex { }`-style seeders. The
user-facing entry points are the macro placeholders `Box.moduleHere`, `Box.computeModuleHere`,
`Box.meshModuleHere`, `Box.rayTracingModuleHere` and `Box.shadertoyHere`; each one throws
`MacroNotExpandedException` if actually called, because `MacroRegistry` is expected to rewrite it
into the real `_moduleHere`-family call.

Before compilation every stage goes through `preprocess`, which resolves `{% include %}` template
tags against other boxes' shader properties (with cycle detection and `#line` fixups) and against
built-in includes such as the field probe, field stats and quantile warp. Registered include roots —
`registerShaderFilesystemIncludeRoot` for a directory, `registerLygiaIncludeRoot` /
`shaderCachedUrlIncludeRootResolver` for URL-fetched, disk-cached libraries — are **not** reachable
from here: they are resolved by shaderc during compilation, from a real `#include` only. It also expands
`{% copyPC %}` (copying a previous stage's push-constant block) and stackAuto template slots
compiled from StackSL via `stackAutoShaderSource`.

`reloadShader`, `reloadComputeShader`, `reloadMeshShader` and `reloadRayTracingShader` are the
reload path: compile, report errors back onto the box's source lines, introspect the result, and
rewrite the box's Kotlin preamble with generated binding structures before swapping the module.
`Box.attachShader` adopts an externally built module into that same path. `Box.fieldProbeHere`,
`Box.fieldStatsHere` and `Box.fieldProbeAutoControl` attach the GPU readback instrumentation.

Everything here needs a live `Box` — properties, error reporting, preamble edits and the
generation-guarded async reload all key off it.

UBO members deliberately get *less* than that: the block itself becomes a `val ModulePointer.<name> by FromUniform()` and each member a `var Structure.<name>`, with no `Mesh`/`MeshGroup` accessor, so a UBO member is written through the uniform rather than per-mesh.
